title: TIMELAPSE OF THE END OF THE UNIVERSE
subtitle: a journey to the last moment

lines.text: In the next thirty minutes, you will watch the sun swallow the Earth, the last star flicker out, and the final black hole in existence evaporate into nothing.
And at the very end, in the dark after everything, you will see why scientists think this story might begin again.
This is mindwired.
Timelapse of the end of the universe. A journey to the last moment.
Here is how this works. We are going to run the clock forward, and never stop.
Watch the counter. Every few seconds, the speed of time doubles.
At first, centuries will crawl past. Then millennia. Then the ages of stars.
By the end, a trillion years will pass in the space of a single breath.
Everything you are about to see is real physics, projected forward by working cosmologists.
Some of it was only discovered in the last two years, and it changes the ending. We will get there.
Where the science is still a hypothesis, we will say so. The rest is settled arithmetic.
Take one last look at the universe as it is now. Bright, warm, and crowded with stars.
You will not see it like this again.
Ten thousand years from now.
Ten thousand years is longer than every written word, every city, every recorded human civilization combined.
And yet, look up. The night sky has barely changed at all.
The constellations have drifted slightly out of shape, like a photograph left in the sun.
Orion's shoulders have shifted. The Big Dipper's handle has bent into a new curve.
Down on Earth, Niagara Falls has eroded itself out of existence, cutting all the way back to its lake.
Every satellite we ever launched into low orbit has long since fallen and burned.
The pyramids, if anything remains of them, are now twice as old as they were.
Voyager 1, still coasting outward, has traveled less than half a light year from home.
On this timescale, humanity's entire story so far is the first frame of the film.
The North Star has changed, too. Earth's axis wobbles like a spinning top, tracing a slow circle.
Polaris has handed the job to another star, the way it inherited it from one before.
The stars have not noticed us yet. Ten thousand years means nothing to a star.
A red dwarf like Proxima Centauri will burn for trillions more years without blinking.
Small things drift. Big things wait. That is the rhythm of the universe at this scale.
But what happens when we stop counting in thousands, and start counting in millions?
One million years from now.
Betelgeuse is long gone. The red supergiant in Orion detonated hundreds of thousands of years ago.
For weeks, its supernova burned in Earth's sky brighter than the full moon.
It was visible in broad daylight, a second sun hanging on the shoulder of a broken constellation.
Now only a spinning corpse remains, a neutron star flickering where a giant once stood.
The constellations you learned as a child no longer exist in any recognizable form.
Every star has wandered. The sky is a stranger now.
On Earth, Meteor Crater in Arizona has eroded away completely. The planet erases its own scars.
No structure built by human hands survives one million years of rain, ice, and plate tectonics.
Except two. The Voyager probes still drift between the stars, dead and perfectly preserved.
Their golden records, built to last a billion years, may now be the oldest human-made objects in existence.
Two whispers in an ocean of night, outlasting everything ever built on Earth.
The moon has drifted about thirty meters farther away. It leaves us slowly, four centimeters a year.
If our descendants are still out there, they live under a sky we would not recognize.
And this is still the very beginning. What does one hundred times longer look like?
One hundred million years from now.
Saturn is losing its crown.
The rings are not permanent. They are younger than the dinosaurs, and they are raining down onto the planet.
Ring particles, tugged by gravity and charged by sunlight, spiral inward as a steady icy rain.
Within a few hundred million years, the most beautiful structure in the solar system simply dissolves.
We were lucky. We existed in the brief window when Saturn had rings at all.
Earth, meanwhile, has been playing cosmic roulette.
Over one hundred million years, there is roughly a coin-flip chance of another impact like the one that killed the dinosaurs.
The continents have wandered. The Atlantic is wider, the Pacific narrower, and new mountains rise where seas used to be.
Whatever maps of Earth ever existed, they now describe a planet that no longer exists.
Out in the galaxy, our solar system has drifted through entire spiral arms.
Dinosaurs to now, that was one hundred million years. Run that whole story again, and we arrive here.
The sun burns on, but it is quietly getting hotter. And that changes everything.
Because the next stop is where Earth's story starts to end.
One billion years from now.
The sun is now about ten percent brighter than it was in your lifetime. That is enough.
Enough to break the Earth.
The oceans are evaporating. Water vapor floods the upper atmosphere, trapping heat in a runaway spiral.
Sunlight splits the vapor apart, and the hydrogen leaks away into space, atom by atom.
The seas that birthed every living thing are boiling off into the dark.
Earth is becoming a desert world, its ocean basins cracked open like dried mud under a furious sky.
By 1.3 billion years, complex life is finished. Only single-celled microbes remain, hiding underground.
Life on Earth ends the way it began. Alone, microscopic, and in the dark.
Here is the cruel accounting. Earth was habitable for roughly five and a half billion years, total.
Life used almost all of it just getting to brains. We arrived minutes before closing time.
Meanwhile, the outer solar system is warming.
The icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn, frozen for eons, begin to soften.
For a brief window, moons like Europa may hold liquid water on their surfaces.
The habitable zone is migrating outward, like a campfire's warmth reaching the back rows.
Life's last refuge in this solar system may not be a planet at all, but a moon.
But refuges only last as long as the campfire. And the campfire is about to explode in size.
Four billion years from now.
For decades, every documentary told you the same story about this moment.
That the Andromeda galaxy, a trillion stars strong, would collide with the Milky Way. Guaranteed.
The textbooks said it was certain. Then, in 2025, we re-ran the numbers.
A study in Nature Astronomy, using better data on our neighboring galaxies, found the odds are only about fifty-fifty within ten billion years.
The most famous collision in astronomy is a coin flip. The universe kept that secret through a century of textbooks.
So flip the coin. Heads, and this happens.
Two spiral galaxies, hundreds of billions of suns each, falling through one another.
Almost no stars actually hit. Space is too empty. The stars pass like ships in a harbor at night.
But gravity rewrites everything. Spiral arms are torn loose and flung across a hundred thousand light years.
Gas clouds slam together and ignite. A firestorm of newborn stars lights up the wreckage.
The two galaxies swing apart, fall back, and merge into one enormous elliptical blur.
Astronomers named the child Milkdromeda. One galaxy, made of two ghosts.
Tails, and the giants waltz past each other, still bound, saving the merger for a later eon.
Either way, they likely end up as one. The coin only decides when.
But while the galaxies dance, something much closer to home is running out of time.
Eight billion years from now.
The sun's core has exhausted the last of its hydrogen. And the sun begins to die.
It does not go quietly. It swells.
At its peak, about 7.9 billion years from now, the sun is 256 times wider than the star you were born under.
Mercury is swallowed. Venus is swallowed. The sun's boiling surface climbs toward Earth's orbit.
And around 7.6 billion years from now, most models agree, it reaches us.
Earth's thin escape routes fail. Tidal drag pulls the planet down into the fire.
The world where everything you have ever loved happened, ends here. Dissolved into the outer layers of its own star.
The dying sun exhales those layers into space, a glowing shroud of gas.
For a few thousand years, our star becomes a planetary nebula, one of the most beautiful objects in the galaxy.
Then the light fades, and only the core remains. A white dwarf.
An Earth-sized ember holding 54 percent of the sun's mass, a million times denser than water.
Somewhere in its ash are the atoms that used to be Mercury, Venus, and Earth.
Everything the inner solar system ever was, filed away in a stellar ash heap.
The outer planets remain. Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune, loyal and dark, orbiting a corpse.
A visitor arriving now would never guess this system once hosted a civilization.
Unless they found the probes. Two golden records, still waiting to be played.
The sun does not explode. It is not massive enough for that. It simply retires, and starts to cool.
It will spend longer as this fading ember than it ever spent as a star.
Our main character is dead, and the story is not even one percent finished.
So what happens to a universe that keeps expanding after its stars start dying?
One hundred billion years from now.
The universe is now seven times older than it was when humans existed.
And something terrible has happened to the sky. It is emptying.
Dark energy has been stretching space faster and faster, and distant galaxies are losing the race.
One by one, they cross the cosmic horizon, the point beyond which their light can never reach us again.
They are not destroyed. They are simply cut off. Forever.
Watch a distant galaxy approach the horizon and its light stretches, reddens, and freezes.
Its final image hangs in the sky like a photograph, fading slowly to black.
Trillions of galaxies exit the universe this way. Politely. Without a sound.
Every galaxy beyond our local group has now vanished past the edge of the observable universe.
Milkdromeda has swallowed its remaining neighbors and floats alone in the dark.
An astronomer born in this era, with perfect telescopes, would see one galaxy and then nothing.
They could never discover the Big Bang. The evidence has physically left their sky.
They would be geniuses, and they would be wrong, because the truth abandoned them.
Think about what that means for us. What evidence has already left ours?
Knowledge in this universe has an expiration date. We are reading the library while it burns.
And the stars themselves are now on their final generation. Who lights the lamps after the last one?
One trillion years from now.
The galaxy is running out of fuel.
Here is a secret about our own time. The universe's star-birth rate peaked ten billion years ago.
You were not born at the dawn of the universe. You were born in its epilogue, while the credits were already rolling.
Now even the epilogue is ending. Star formation needs cold gas, and the cold gas is nearly gone.
Somewhere in Milkdromeda, one of the last star-forming clouds collapses and ignites.
A handful of final newborn stars, small and red, lighting up in a galaxy of retirees.
These late children are red dwarfs, tiny misers that sip their fuel for trillions of years.
The universe's strategy has changed. No more bonfires. Only candles, rationed to last.
Strange collisions still light the darkness now and then. Two dead white dwarfs spiral together and reignite.
For a moment, a new star burns where no star should exist, assembled from corpses.
These resurrection stars will be the only new lights for trillions of years to come.
The age of abundant starlight, the Stelliferous Era, is entering its long final act.
Every star that will ever be born now exists. From here, the count only goes down.
Down, and down, until one night there is exactly one star left. What does that night look like?
One hundred trillion years from now.
This is the night the last star dies.
Somewhere in the darkness, a final red dwarf has been burning for trillions of years.
Red dwarfs do not explode. They do not even swell into red giants. They are too small, too careful for that.
This one has stirred every last atom of its hydrogen into the fire, grown hotter, bluer, and simply run dry.
Its light flickers, dims, and goes out.
And with it ends the era of stars. Ten thousand times longer than all of cosmic history before it.
Nothing shines anymore. Anywhere.
The universe now contains only remnants. White dwarfs, neutron stars, black holes, and frozen wandering planets.
Cosmologists call what comes next the Degenerate Era, named for the exhausted matter that remains.
If you were standing on one of the surviving planets now, this is what you would see.
Nothing. A sky of perfect black, no stars, no glow, no horizon. Your own hand invisible in front of your face.
Under your feet, a world frozen within a whisper of absolute zero, holding the fossils of an atmosphere.
The neutron stars persist. City-sized spheres of pure nuclear matter, spinning in the dark.
Some still pulse their lighthouse beams across a universe with no ships left to warn.
Even the magnetars, the most violent magnets nature ever built, have gone quiet.
If life still exists, it huddles around white dwarfs, harvesting the last warmth in the cosmos.
But even embers cool. And the darkness is patient.
What does gravity do with a universe full of corpses and infinite time to play with?
Ten to the power twenty years from now. One hundred billion billion years.
The galaxies themselves are dissolving.
Over these absurd timescales, close encounters between dead stars slowly fling them out of the galaxy.
First the planets are stripped from their dead suns, detached by passing stars and set adrift.
Then the stars themselves. Somewhere between ninety and ninety-nine percent of all remnants are ejected into the void.
Star by star, Milkdromeda is evaporating into intergalactic space.
The rest spiral inward, and fall into the supermassive black hole at the center.
The black hole grows fat on the wreckage of a hundred billion dead suns.
Rogue black holes cruise the darkness, invisible, swallowing anything unlucky enough to cross them.
The white dwarfs have finished cooling. They no longer emit visible light at all.
They are black dwarfs now. Objects so far in our future that not one exists yet, anywhere in the universe.
Each one has cooled to about five degrees above absolute zero. Colder than your freezer, with the mass of a star.
Put yourself in orbit around one. You would never see it. You would only feel it, a blind weight in the dark, swinging you around an invisible point forever.
If Earth's cinder escaped the sun, it drifts out here somewhere. A silent stone circling a silent ember, going nowhere, forever.
The universe has become a museum with the lights off, and gravity is quietly stealing the exhibits.
But the exhibits themselves may not be safe. Because matter itself might have an expiration date.
Ten to the power thirty-four years and beyond.
Now we reach the deepest question in this entire journey. Does matter last forever?
Many physicists suspect it does not. They suspect the proton, the heart of every atom, eventually decays.
Be clear. This is a hypothesis. Proton decay has never been observed, despite decades of watching.
In Japan, fifty thousand tons of ultra-pure water sit in darkness, ringed by thousands of golden light sensors.
Scientists have watched that tank for decades, waiting for a single proton to flash goodbye.
Not one ever has. We now know protons live at least ten to the power thirty-four years, and an even bigger detector is listening right now.
But most grand unified theories of physics insist that eventually, every proton must fall apart.
If they are right, then out here in deep time, the end of matter begins.
Inside every black dwarf, every frozen planet, every drifting rock, protons quietly wink out of existence.
Each decay releases a tiny flash of energy. The dead stars gain a final, impossible warmth.
Proton decay keeps each black dwarf a few degrees above absolute zero. That trickle is the last heat source in the universe.
It is less power than a household light bulb, spread across an entire dead star. And it is everything.
Slowly, atom by atom, every solid object in existence evaporates into positrons and radiation.
The planets dissolve. The black dwarfs dissolve. Every monument, every fossil, every atom that was ever you.
By ten to the power forty years, if the theories are right, matter as we know it is over.
And a strange footnote. If protons never decay, physics has an even slower ending on file.
Over ten to the power fifteen hundred years, quantum tunneling would slowly transmute all matter into iron.
Dead stars would become iron stars, the most stable objects arithmetic allows.
Either way, the destination is the same. Matter simplifies, settles, and surrenders.
Nothing made of atoms remains. So what is left, when matter itself is gone?
Ten to the power forty years from now.
The black holes. Only the things that were never made of atoms survive the death of atoms.
Welcome to the Black Hole Era. The universe now belongs entirely to them.
Every galaxy that ever existed is now, at most, a single black hole and a thin fog of particles.
The monsters have inherited everything. And the largest of them are beyond imagining.
Remember TON 618, the sixty-six billion solar mass giant we could see from Earth?
Holes like that now drift through the darkness, horizons wider than entire ancient solar systems.
Nothing orbits them anymore. There is nothing left to orbit.
They do not feed. They do not grow. They simply exist, holding everything they ever swallowed.
An event horizon is the universe's most patient archive. Whatever fell in is still accounted for.
Somewhere inside them, in whatever form information takes past a horizon, is the ledger of everything that ever fell.
Stars, planets, oceans. Possibly the atoms of everyone who ever lived.
The black holes are the universe's last libraries.
For a span of time that dwarfs everything that came before, nothing happens at all.
No collisions. No light. No change. Just black spheres in black space, outnumbered by nothing.
If you think this is the end, you are wrong. Because black holes have a secret.
Stephen Hawking found it. They are not eternal.
They leak.
And the fire that burns the last libraries has already been lit. How long can they hold out?
Ten to the power sixty-seven years from now.
Quantum physics does not allow even a black hole to keep everything forever.
At the edge of every event horizon, space itself simmers with particles flickering in and out of existence.
Occasionally one escapes, stealing a whisper of the black hole's mass as it goes.
This is Hawking radiation. A black hole the mass of our sun glows at sixty billionths of a degree. And it is utterly relentless.
A solar-mass black hole takes ten to the power sixty-seven years to evaporate. Every year since the Big Bang is a rounding error against that number.
But this timelapse does not stop. So watch.
The black hole shrinks. And shrinking makes it hotter, which makes it shrink faster.
Slowly at first. Over eons, the glow sharpens.
The stellar black holes go first, each ending in a burst of gamma rays.
One by one, across an eternity, the archives of the universe burn their contents and close.
The supermassive monsters hold out the longest. A giant like TON 618 lasts nearly ten to the power one hundred years.
A one followed by one hundred zeros. A googol. There are not a googol atoms in the observable universe. There are not a googol anythings. Except years.
And now, somewhere in the darkness, the last black hole in the universe is dying.
It has outlived everything. Stars, galaxies, matter itself. It is the final object in existence.
Its horizon tightens. Its glow climbs from billionths of a degree toward a final fever.
If you could stand witness, you would see the only light in the universe. A single point, brightening in an infinite black, like the last coal of a fire that once filled everything.
In its final second, it releases the energy of a million hydrogen bombs.
A flash.
The last event horizon evaporates, and the last thing that could ever be called a thing, is gone.
The universe's final firework, with no one and nothing left to see it.
Silence.
Beyond ten to the power one hundred years.
This is the Dark Era. It is the universe's final state, and it lasts, as far as we know, forever.
Nothing remains but stray photons, neutrinos, electrons, and positrons, drifting through expanding emptiness.
The average distance between particles is now larger than the entire observable universe of our time.
Occasionally, an electron and a positron find each other and fall into orbit. An atom of positronium, larger than a galaxy.
A single orbit takes longer than the entire age of stars. It is the last slow dance in existence.
Nothing has a temperature anymore. Nothing has a location worth naming. Nothing happens.
This is heat death. Not fire, not collapse. Just perfect, uniform, eternal stillness.
Time still passes, technically. But time only means anything when things change, and nothing changes.
Past ten to the power twenty-five hundred years, physics simply runs out of predictions. The map ends here.
The story that began with the Big Bang, that built galaxies and oceans and minds, ends in a place with no story at all.
At least, that is the ending we believed in. Until a few years ago.
Because the end of the universe was rewritten while you were alive.
In the mid-2020s, an instrument called DESI mapped tens of millions of galaxies to measure dark energy across cosmic history.
And it found hints, growing toward four sigma, that dark energy is not constant. It may be weakening.
Every ending you just watched assumes dark energy stays fixed forever. If it evolves, all bets are off.
A weakening push could slow the expansion. Change it enough, and the universe could even recollapse, ending in fire instead of ice.
Melodysheep could not have known this. The textbooks are being rewritten right now, in your lifetime, and the final chapter is genuinely open.
The old rivals have weakened, too. The Big Rip, dark energy tearing space apart, is now disfavored by that same data.
Vacuum decay, a bubble of new physics erasing everything at light speed, stays possible but is expected to wait past ten to the power one hundred years.
The apocalypse you would never see coming is, mercifully, in no hurry.
So the quiet ending remains the default. Expansion, dilution, darkness.
Not with a bang. With an endless, dimming whisper.
But even that whisper may not be the last word.
Because even perfect emptiness is not truly empty.
Quantum mechanics forbids absolute stillness. The vacuum itself always trembles, everywhere, forever.
And given infinite time, even the most absurdly improbable tremble eventually happens.
Some physicists speculate that a large enough quantum fluctuation could seed something extraordinary.
A new inflation event. A new bubble of spacetime, inflating out of the ashes of ours.
This is speculation stacked on speculation. Be honest about that. No one knows.
But if it is possible, then somewhere in that infinite quiet, it is inevitable.
There are other doors out of the dark. Some cosmologists propose cyclic universes, endlessly renewing, with our eon just one heartbeat.
Roger Penrose has argued that a totally empty universe forgets its own scale, and becomes a new beginning.
In his picture, the infinitely far future and a new Big Bang are literally the same thing.
And mathematics offers one last door. Wait ten to the power ten to the power ten to the power fifty-six years, and physics suggests arrangements of matter could recur.
That is the largest number with a physical meaning ever written down. And infinity dwarfs it.
None of this is proven. All of it is honest physics, published, argued, and unresolved.
A flicker in the dark. A point of impossible heat. And then, expansion.
A newborn universe, igniting with its own Big Bang, growing its own galaxies, its own stars.
Perhaps its own oceans. Perhaps its own minds, looking up and asking how it all began.
Perhaps this has already happened. Perhaps our own Big Bang was exactly this.
The last moment of one universe, and the first moment of the next, might be the same moment.
The end of time might just be time, clearing its throat.
Now come back.
Back past the dark era, the dying black holes, the dissolving atoms, the last star.
Back past the frozen Earth, the swollen sun, the waltzing galaxies.
Back to a small blue planet, in a bright young galaxy, 13.8 billion years after the beginning.
Back to now. Back to you.
Here is the thing this entire journey was building to.
Run the numbers on everything you just watched. Compare the age of stars to the eternity that follows.
Life like ours is possible for only the thinnest sliver at the very start of the universe's story.
Physicist Brian Cox put it this way. The arrow of time creates a brief window in which life can exist. This is that window.
You are not living at some random point in eternity. You are living in the flash at the very beginning.
The universe is not ancient. Compared to what is coming, it has barely opened its eyes.
You live in the era of light. The brief, dazzling age when stars burn and skies are full.
The age when the universe can still be seen, still be read, still be understood.
Beings in the far future, if any exist, would trade anything to see what you see tonight.
A sky full of stars is not normal. It is a temporary miracle, and you were born inside it.
Every sunrise you have ever ignored is a spectacle the last nine-tenths of eternity will never get.
And here is the strangest comfort of all. Nothing that happens in this video erases you.
The future does not delete the past. It only comes after it.
Ten to the power one hundred years from now, it will still be true that you existed.
That you lived on a blue world, under a young sun, in the era when the universe was awake.
The heat death cannot touch that. Nothing can.
The universe spent 13.8 billion years arranging atoms into something that could watch its own ending and feel awe.
You are not small. You are the part of the universe that noticed.
lines.arg: YOU ARE THE PART THAT NOTICED

lines.text: So look up. While there is still everything to see.
This has been a journey of ten to the power one hundred years, and it fit inside your evening.
If it changed the way tonight's sky looks to you, subscribe to mindwired.
We will be here until the last star goes out. See you in the next one.
